definition: Splitting networking into a stack of layers, each with one job, that uses the service of the layer below and offers a simpler service to the layer above. It lets Ethernet, IP, TCP and HTTP be designed and replaced independently.
example: HTTP does not need to know whether its bytes cross fibre or Wi-Fi, because the layers below hide that.

definition: The Open Systems Interconnection model: a seven-layer reference model from the ISO (International Organization for Standardization). Its own protocols were little used, but its layer numbers (layer 2, layer 3, layer 7) are still how engineers name devices and functions.
example: A "layer 7 load balancer" reads application data such as HTTP; a "layer 2 switch" uses only Ethernet addresses.

definition: The four-layer model of the protocols the internet actually runs: link, internet, transport and application. It is described in RFC 1122 and named after its two best-known protocols, TCP and IP.
example: In the TCP/IP model, TLS and HTTP both sit in the application layer.

definition: A teaching model used by textbooks such as Kurose and Ross: physical, link, network, transport and application. It is the TCP/IP model with the link layer split into a physical layer and a link layer.
example: This subject uses the five-layer model, so "layer 2" means the link layer and "layer 3" the network layer.

definition: Layer 1: turns bits into signals on a medium (voltages on copper, light in fibre, radio waves) and back again. It decides symbol rates, line codes, connectors and cable reach.
example: 1000BASE-T and 10GBASE-SR are two different physical layers that both carry Ethernet frames.

definition: Layer 2: moves a frame across one link or one LAN to the next device, using link-specific framing and, on Ethernet and Wi-Fi, MAC addresses. It is hop-by-hop: each link gets a fresh frame.
example: A router strips the incoming Ethernet frame and builds a new one, with new MAC addresses, for the next link.

definition: Layer 3: carries packets from a source host to a destination host across many links, using IP addresses and routing. Every router on the path reads this layer.
example: IPv4 and IPv6 are network-layer protocols; routers forward on the destination IP address.

definition: Layer 4: delivers data between programs on two hosts, identified by port numbers. TCP adds reliability, ordering and congestion control; UDP adds little beyond ports and a checksum.
example: A web browser and a web server talk over the transport layer using TCP port 443.

definition: The top layer: the protocols programs use directly, such as HTTP for web pages, DNS for names and SMTP for mail.
example: An HTTP GET request is an application-layer message.

definition: OSI layer 6, meant for data representation: encodings, compression and encryption. The TCP/IP model has no separate presentation layer; applications and libraries such as TLS do this work.
example: Character encoding (such as UTF-8) is presentation-style work done inside the application.

definition: OSI layer 5, meant for managing dialogues (sessions) between applications. The TCP/IP model has no separate session layer; applications handle sessions themselves.
example: An application that resumes a login session after a reconnect is doing session-layer work itself.

definition: Request for Comments: the numbered document series, published by the RFC Editor, that holds internet standards and related notes. Protocols such as IP, TCP and ARP are defined in RFCs.
example: ARP is defined in RFC 826 (1982); the TCP window scale option in RFC 7323.

definition: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: the application-layer protocol mail servers use to send email to each other.
example: Your mail server uses SMTP to hand a message to the recipient's mail server.

definition: The network-layer protocol of the internet. It carries packets from a source IP address to a destination IP address across many links, with no guarantee of delivery or order. IPv4 and IPv6 are its two versions.
example: An IP packet keeps the same source and destination IP addresses across every router on an ordinary path.

definition: Internet Control Message Protocol: IP's companion for error and diagnostic messages, such as "destination unreachable", "packet too big" and the echo request used by ping. ICMPv6 also carries IPv6 Neighbor Discovery.
example: A router that cannot forward an oversized packet may send back an ICMP message saying what size would fit.

definition: The dominant family of wired link-layer technologies, standardised as IEEE 802.3. It defines a frame format with 48-bit MAC addresses and many physical layers, from 10 Mbit/s to 400 Gbit/s and beyond. "Ethernet II" names the common frame format whose type field is an EtherType.
example: A desktop plugged into a wall socket with a copper cable is almost certainly using Ethernet.

definition: The family of wireless LAN standards, IEEE 802.11, that carries Ethernet-like frames over radio. Wi-Fi 6 is the marketing name for 802.11ax.
example: A laptop on Wi-Fi shares the radio channel with every other device on the same access point.

definition: Local area network: a network covering one building or site, such as an office or home, usually Ethernet and Wi-Fi joined by switches.
example: Every device on a home LAN can reach every other without going through the internet.

definition: The link layer's unit of data: a header (addresses and type), a payload, and usually a trailer with an error check. Each link carries its own frame; a router builds a new one for the next link.
example: An Ethernet frame is between 64 and 1518 bytes in its basic untagged form.

definition: The network layer's unit of data: an IP header plus a payload such as a TCP segment. A packet keeps its IP header from source to destination while each link wraps it in a new frame.
example: A full-size Ethernet link carries IP packets of up to 1500 bytes.

definition: TCP's unit of data: a TCP header followed by a slice of the byte stream. It travels as the payload of an IP packet.
example: With a 1500-byte IP packet and minimal headers, a TCP segment carries 1460 bytes of data.

definition: A self-contained message sent without a connection or delivery guarantee. UDP's unit of data is called a datagram, and IP packets are sometimes called datagrams too.
example: A DNS query usually travels in a single UDP datagram.

definition: The data a protocol carries for the layer above, as opposed to its own header and trailer. One layer's whole message is the next layer down's payload.
example: An Ethernet payload is 46 to 1500 bytes and usually holds an IP packet.

definition: Control information a protocol puts in front of its payload: addresses, lengths, type fields, sequence numbers and checksums. Each layer adds its own header on the way down and removes it on the way up.
example: A minimal TCP header is 20 bytes and a minimal IPv4 header another 20.

definition: Wrapping one layer's data inside the next layer's unit by adding a header (and sometimes a trailer). On receipt, each layer removes its own header and passes the rest upwards.
example: HTTP data goes inside a TCP segment, which goes inside an IP packet, which goes inside an Ethernet frame.

definition: Protocol data unit: the name for one layer's unit of data. By convention it is a frame at the link layer, a packet at the network layer, a segment (TCP) or datagram (UDP) at the transport layer, and a message at the application layer.
example: The same bytes are a TCP segment's PDU at layer 4 and part of an IP packet's payload at layer 3.

definition: Deciding, at each layer, which protocol or program should receive the payload, using a field in the header such as EtherType, the IP protocol number or the port number.
example: EtherType 0x86DD sends a frame's payload to IPv6; Next Header 6 then sends it to TCP.

definition: The 2-byte field in an Ethernet II header that names the protocol in the payload. Values of 1536 (0x0600) and above are EtherTypes; 0x0800 is IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6 and 0x0806 ARP.
example: A frame with EtherType 0x0806 carries an ARP message, not an IP packet.

definition: The field in the IPv4 header (called Next Header in IPv6) that says which protocol the payload carries. 6 is TCP, 17 is UDP, 1 is ICMPv4 and 58 is ICMPv6; IANA keeps the registry.
example: A packet with protocol number 17 is handed to UDP.

definition: A 16-bit number (0 to 65,535) in TCP and UDP headers that, with the IP addresses, identifies which program's connection or socket a segment belongs to. Well-known services use conventional ports.
example: HTTPS conventionally uses TCP port 443 and DNS port 53.

definition: Frame check sequence: the 4-byte CRC-32 at the end of an Ethernet frame. The receiver recomputes it and silently drops the frame if it does not match.
example: A frame damaged by noise fails its FCS check and is discarded by the next switch or host.

definition: Cyclic redundancy check: an error-detecting code computed as the remainder of a binary polynomial division (using XOR). It reliably catches short bursts of errors and is cheap in hardware, but offers no protection against deliberate tampering.
example: Ethernet appends a 32-bit CRC to every frame as its FCS.

definition: The 32-bit CRC used by Ethernet, with generator polynomial 0x04C11DB7. It detects every burst error up to 32 bits long, and, per Koopman's tables, every error of 1, 2 or 3 bits in data words up to 91,607 bits long.
example: The standard CRC-32 check value for the ASCII string "123456789" is 0xCBF43926.

definition: A known bit pattern sent at the start of every transmission so the receiver can detect it and lock its clock on before the real data arrives. Ethernet sends 7 bytes of alternating 1s and 0s, not counted in the frame size; Wi-Fi and other radio links use their own, longer PHY preambles.
example: On Ethernet the preamble and SFD together add 8 bytes of wire time to every frame.

definition: Start frame delimiter: the 1-byte pattern after the Ethernet preamble that ends in two 1s, signalling that the frame itself (the destination address) starts next.
example: Preamble (7 bytes) plus SFD (1 byte) make 8 bytes of overhead before each frame.

definition: The idle time Ethernet leaves between frames: nominally 96 bit-times, the time to send 12 bytes. It counts as overhead when working out how many frames a link can carry.
example: At 1 Gbit/s the 96-bit gap lasts 96 ns.

definition: The time a link takes to send one byte (8 bits) at its rate. Wire overheads such as the gap between frames are often counted in byte-times.
example: At 1 Gbit/s one byte-time is 8 ns.

definition: The time a link takes to send one bit: 1 divided by the bit rate. Ethernet timing rules, such as the slot time and the inter-frame gap, are stated in bit-times so they scale with speed.
example: At 10 Mbit/s one bit-time is 0.1 µs; at 1 Gbit/s it is 1 ns.

definition: The physical-layer device, or the physical-layer part of a standard, that turns bits into signals on the medium and back. Different Ethernet PHYs (for copper, multimode fibre, single-mode fibre) carry the same frames.
example: A 10GBASE-SR transceiver and a 10GBASE-T port are different PHYs for the same 10 Gbit/s Ethernet.

definition: Acknowledgement: a message from a receiver telling the sender that data arrived. Reliable protocols such as TCP use ACKs to decide what to send next and what to retransmit.
example: In stop-and-wait, the sender may not send frame 2 until the ACK for frame 1 arrives.

definition: The byte order internet protocol headers use for multi-byte numbers: big-endian, most significant byte first. Python's struct module writes it as "!".
example: The EtherType 0x0800 is sent as the byte 0x08 followed by 0x00.

definition: An address meaning "every station". On Ethernet it is the all-ones MAC address ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff; switches flood such frames to every eligible port in the VLAN.
example: An ARP request is sent to the broadcast MAC so every host on the LAN can see it.

definition: The set of devices that receive each other's link-layer broadcasts: one LAN or one VLAN. Routers, and VLAN boundaries, separate broadcast domains.
example: Two VLANs on the same switch are two separate broadcast domains.

definition: Storing or sending a multi-byte number with its most significant byte first. Internet protocol headers are big-endian, which is why it is also called network byte order.
example: The 16-bit value 0x86DD is sent big-endian as the byte 0x86 followed by 0xDD.

definition: A small value computed from data so the receiver can recompute it and notice accidental changes. IPv4, UDP and TCP use a simple 16-bit sum; it is fast but weaker than a CRC.
example: A router that decrements an IPv4 packet's TTL must update its header checksum too.

definition: A set of IP header fields (source and destination address, protocol number and length) that TCP and UDP include in their checksum without sending them as part of their own header. It ties the segment to the right addresses, but means address translation must fix the checksum.
example: A NAT that rewrites the source IP must also adjust the TCP checksum, because the address is in the pseudo-header.

definition: A form of NAT that rewrites both IP addresses and port numbers so many devices can share one public IP address. The translator keeps a table mapping each inside address and port to an outside port.
example: A home router may map 192.168.1.20 port 51000 to its public address port 62001.

definition: Splitting an IP packet that is too big for the next link into smaller pieces that are reassembled at the destination. IPv4 routers may fragment unless the "don't fragment" flag is set; IPv6 routers never do.
example: A 1500-byte packet entering a link with a 1400-byte MTU must be fragmented or dropped.

definition: The smallest MTU on any link along a path: the largest packet that can cross the whole path without fragmentation. Path MTU discovery finds it using ICMP "too big" messages or by probing.
example: A path through a VPN tunnel may have a path MTU of 1400 bytes even though every physical link is 1500.

definition: A failure where packets above some size silently vanish, usually because a link needs a smaller MTU and the ICMP messages that would tell the sender are filtered. Small packets work, large ones never arrive.
example: A connection opens and then hangs as soon as a full-size data packet is sent.

definition: A device in the network path that does more than forward packets: firewalls, NATs, load balancers, proxies and intrusion detectors. They often inspect transport headers, which makes changing those protocols hard.
example: A firewall that drops TCP segments carrying an unfamiliar option is a middlebox.

definition: A device or program that allows or blocks traffic according to rules, typically based on addresses, ports, protocols and connection state.
example: A firewall might allow only TCP port 443 inbound to a web server.

definition: The loss of freedom to change a protocol because devices in the network depend on its current form, for example middleboxes that drop packets with unfamiliar options. QUIC encrypts much of its header partly to avoid this.
example: New TCP options are hard to deploy because some middleboxes strip or block them.

definition: The state where traffic arriving at a link or router exceeds what it can send, so queues grow and packets are delayed or dropped.
example: An uplink running near 100% utilisation is congested: queues build and latency rises.

definition: The rules a sender such as TCP uses to slow down when the network seems overloaded, so senders share capacity and avoid collapse. Loss-based schemes treat packet loss as the main congestion signal.
example: TCP halves (or similarly reduces) its sending window after detecting a loss.

definition: Multiprotocol Label Switching: a technique, widely used inside carrier networks, that forwards packets by short labels added between the link and IP headers. It is often called "layer 2.5" because it fits neither layer.
example: A provider can carry many customers' traffic across its core using MPLS labels.

definition: Virtual Extensible LAN: a tunnel that carries whole Ethernet frames inside UDP packets (port 4789) across an IP network, with a 24-bit segment ID allowing about 16 million separate networks. Data centres use it to stretch layer 2 over routed fabrics.
example: VXLAN adds 50 bytes (outer IPv4, UDP, VXLAN and inner Ethernet headers) inside the outer IP packet.

definition: Virtual private network: an encrypted tunnel across another network, making remote hosts or sites appear connected to a private network. The tunnel headers reduce the space left for data in each packet.
example: A site-to-site VPN between two offices adds its own headers to every packet, lowering the effective MTU.

definition: Carrying one protocol's packets or frames as the payload of another, such as Ethernet inside UDP (VXLAN) or IP inside an encrypted VPN. Each tunnel adds headers, which shrinks the room left for the inner packet.
example: A tunnel with 50 bytes of overhead on a 1500-byte path leaves 1450 bytes for the inner packet.

definition: The shape of the internet architecture: many link technologies below and many applications above all meet at one network protocol, IP. Anything that can carry IP packets can join the internet.
example: IP runs over Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 5G and satellite links alike, which is the narrow waist at work.

definition: The design argument that some functions, such as reliable delivery or integrity checking, can only be done fully by the two end hosts, because checks in the middle cannot see damage outside their own stretch of the path.
example: Link CRCs miss corruption inside a router's memory, so file transfers still compare an end-to-end hash.

definition: Done separately on each link or at each device along a path, rather than once between the two ends. The link layer is hop-by-hop: every link gets a new frame with new MAC addresses.
example: Ethernet's FCS is checked and regenerated hop-by-hop at every switch or router.

definition: Between the two communicating hosts, across the whole path, rather than link by link. Transport and application headers are, in principle, end-to-end: routers do not need to read them.
example: A TCP connection is end-to-end: the routers in between forward its packets without taking part.

definition: One step along a network path: a link plus the device at its far end. A packet crossing three routers between two hosts makes four hops.
example: traceroute lists the routers at each hop on the way to a destination.

definition: The neighbouring device a packet is sent to next on its way to its destination: either the destination itself on the same subnet, or a router.
example: For a remote destination the next hop is usually the default gateway, so the frame carries the gateway's MAC address.

definition: A network-layer device that forwards IP packets between networks, choosing each packet's next hop from its routing table. It terminates the link layer: each packet leaves in a new frame.
example: A home router forwards packets between the home LAN and the internet provider's network.

definition: Choosing the path packets take across networks, and the network-layer forwarding that follows those choices. Routers decide using destination IP addresses and routing tables.
example: IP routing lets a packet from London reach a server in Frankfurt through a dozen routers.

definition: The operating system object a program uses to send and receive network data. A TCP socket is identified by local and remote IP addresses and ports.
example: A web server has one listening socket on port 443 and one connected socket per client.

definition: The fourth and fifth generations of mobile (cellular) networks. Like Wi-Fi they constantly adapt modulation to radio conditions, and IP runs over them like any other link.
example: A phone streaming video over 5G uses IP over the 5G radio link.

definition: A widely used command-line tool that measures achievable throughput between two hosts by sending test traffic.
example: Running iperf3 between two servers on a clean gigabit link typically reports a little under 950 Mbit/s of TCP payload.

definition: The HTTP request header naming the website the client wants, such as Host: example.com. It lets one server or load balancer host many sites on one IP address.
example: A load balancer reads the Host header to send shop.example.com and api.example.com to different backends.

definition: The second major version of HTTP: a binary protocol that sends many requests at once over one connection. It was deployed without any change to Ethernet or IP, an example of layering working.
example: A browser fetching 50 images over HTTP/2 can use a single TCP connection.

definition: Stream Control Transmission Protocol: a transport protocol with its own IP protocol number (132) offering reliable, message-oriented multi-stream delivery. Many NATs and firewalls do not pass it, which limits its use on the internet.
example: SCTP is used inside telephone signalling networks but rarely across the public internet.

definition: The part of a computer where ordinary programs run, outside the operating system kernel. A protocol over UDP, such as QUIC, can be implemented in user space and updated with the application.
example: Browsers ship their own QUIC code in user space instead of waiting for operating system updates.

definition: A QUIC header field that identifies a connection independently of IP addresses and ports, so a connection can survive a change of network. It is visible to the network, unlike most of QUIC's header.
example: A phone moving from Wi-Fi to 5G can keep its QUIC connection because the connection ID stays the same.

aliases: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
definition: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, the body whose 802 committee writes the Ethernet (802.3), Wi-Fi (802.11) and bridging and VLAN (802.1) standards. It also assigns OUIs for MAC addresses.
example: IEEE 802.1Q defines VLAN tagging.

definition: A widely used open-source operating system kernel, running most servers and many network devices. Its networking commands include ip neigh for the ARP cache.
example: On Linux, ip neigh shows the neighbour (ARP) cache.

definition: The lower part of the link layer that frames data, addresses it with MAC addresses and decides when a station may transmit on the medium. In this subject "MAC" on its own usually means a MAC address, the 48-bit link-layer address of an Ethernet or Wi-Fi interface; in security protocols such as SSH and TLS it instead means a message authentication code.
example: A "destination MAC" is the destination MAC address in an Ethernet header.

definition: The smallest unit of information: a 0 or a 1. Network link rates are counted in bits per second, while file sizes are usually in bytes, so multiply bytes by 8 to compare them.
example: A 1500-byte packet is 12,000 bits.

definition: A group of 8 bits, the unit for packet and file sizes. Network standards often call it an octet to be unambiguous.
example: A 100 Mbit/s link moves at most 12.5 million bytes per second.

definition: Sending to exactly one destination. A unicast MAC address has its I/G (individual/group) bit set to 0.
example: An ARP reply is unicast straight back to the host that asked.

definition: Sending to a group of interested receivers at once. A multicast MAC address has its I/G bit set to 1, so its first byte is odd.
example: 01:00:5e:00:00:fb is an Ethernet multicast address used for IPv4 mDNS.

definition: The rate at which data actually gets through a link or path, in bits per second, as opposed to the link's nominal rate. It is limited by the slowest link (the bottleneck), by window size and RTT, and by competing traffic.
example: A 1 Gbit/s home network behind 100 Mbit/s broadband gets at most 100 Mbit/s of throughput to the internet.

definition: Throughput counting only useful application data, delivered once: it excludes headers, framing, retransmitted copies and control messages. It is always below the link rate.
example: A clean gigabit Ethernet link with full-size TCP segments gives about 949 Mbit/s of goodput before application overhead.

definition: How many bits per second a link can put onto the wire: its nominal speed, such as 1 Gbit/s. "Line rate" also means running a device at the link's full rate.
example: A firewall that handles "10 Gbit/s line rate" must keep up even when the link is full of small frames.

definition: The unit of data rate: how many bits pass a point each second. Networks use decimal prefixes: kbit/s (thousand), Mbit/s (million), Gbit/s (billion).
example: 100 Mbit/s is 100,000,000 bits per second, at most 12.5 million bytes per second.

definition: Kilobits per second: thousands of bits per second (1 kbit/s = 1,000 bit/s).
example: A stop-and-wait sender on a gigabit link across a country manages only about 400 kbit/s.

definition: Megabits per second: millions of bits per second (1 Mbit/s = 1,000,000 bit/s). Broadband speeds are usually quoted in Mbit/s; divide by 8 for megabytes per second.
example: A 100 Mbit/s connection downloads at most 12.5 MB per second.

definition: Gigabits per second: billions of bits per second (1 Gbit/s = 10⁹ bit/s). Common for wired Ethernet links; "gigabit Ethernet" runs at 1 Gbit/s.
example: At 1 Gbit/s a 1500-byte packet takes 12 µs to transmit.

definition: Terabits per second: 10¹² bits per second, the scale of total capacity on a modern fibre carrying many wavelengths.
example: A fibre with 80 wavelengths at 100 Gbit/s each carries 8 Tbit/s.

definition: A unit of data size: in decimal, 1,000,000 bytes (8,000,000 bits). Some software uses MB for the binary 1,048,576 bytes, properly called a mebibyte (MiB).
example: A 500 MB file is 4,000 Mbit.

definition: A unit of data size: in decimal, 1,000 bytes. Sometimes used loosely for 1,024 bytes, properly called a kibibyte (KiB).
example: A 20 KB API response is 160,000 bits.

definition: A unit of data size: in decimal, 10⁹ bytes (8 × 10⁹ bits).
example: A 1 GB download at 100 Mbit/s takes 80 s of transmission.

definition: A binary unit of data size: 1 KiB is 1,024 bytes and 1 MiB is 1,048,576 bytes. Binary units are common for memory and file sizes; network rates use decimal units.
example: 64 KiB is 65,536 bytes, one more than TCP's unscaled window limit of 65,535.

definition: A thousandth of a second (10⁻³ s). Round-trip times across countries and continents are tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
example: Light in fibre needs about 1 ms per 200 km.

definition: A millionth of a second (10⁻⁶ s). Transmission and propagation over short links are measured in microseconds.
example: A signal in fibre travels about 1 km in 5 µs.

definition: A billionth of a second (10⁻⁹ s).
example: At 1 Gbit/s one bit lasts 1 ns; light covers about 30 cm in that time.

definition: The unit of speed. Signals travel at about 2 × 10⁸ m/s (200,000 km/s) in glass fibre and close to 3 × 10⁸ m/s in air.
example: 3,000 km at 200,000 km/s takes 15 ms.

definition: A thousand metres. Fibre loss and propagation delay are usually stated per kilometre.
example: A loss of 0.2 dB/km over 80 km is 16 dB.

definition: A billionth of a metre, the unit for light wavelengths. Fibre optics use infrared light around 850 nm (multimode) and 1310 or 1550 nm (single-mode).
example: Single-mode long-haul links usually run near 1550 nm, where glass loses least light.

definition: A millionth of a metre. Fibre core diameters are measured in micrometres.
example: Multi-mode fibre cores are 50 or 62.5 µm across; a single-mode core is about 9 µm.

definition: The time to push all of a packet's bits onto a link: packet length in bits divided by link rate in bits per second. It depends on size and rate, not distance.
example: A 1500-byte packet takes 120 µs to transmit at 100 Mbit/s.

definition: The time a signal takes to travel the length of a link: distance divided by signal speed. It depends on distance and medium, not on packet size or link rate.
example: A 3,000 km fibre has about 15 ms of propagation delay each way.

definition: Time a packet spends waiting in a buffer behind other packets before it can be transmitted. Zero on an idle link, it can reach hundreds of milliseconds when a link is overloaded.
example: At 90% utilisation the simple M/M/1 model predicts an average wait of 9 packet times.

definition: Time a device spends examining a packet's header, deciding where to send it and checking it for errors.
example: A router might take tens of microseconds to process a packet, depending on its hardware and features.

definition: Forwarding in which a switch or router receives a whole frame or packet, checks it, and only then starts sending it on. Transmission delay is therefore paid again on every link.
example: Three store-and-forward links at 3 ms of transmission each take 9 ms in total.

definition: Forwarding that starts sending a frame on as soon as its destination address has been read, before the rest arrives. It lowers latency but can pass on frames later found to be corrupt.
example: A cut-through switch can start forwarding after reading the first 6 bytes of a frame, the destination MAC.

definition: Variation in packet delay from one packet to the next. Queueing is a common cause; video calls and games suffer when jitter is high.
example: Packets arriving 20 ms, 80 ms and 35 ms after sending show a 60 ms spread in delay (peak-to-peak jitter).

definition: Memory in a router, switch or host that holds packets waiting to be sent or read. Buffers absorb bursts but add delay when they fill.
example: A sender needs socket buffers at least as large as the bandwidth-delay product to fill a long, fast path.

definition: Excessive delay caused by oversized buffers in routers and modems that let queues grow to hundreds of milliseconds instead of dropping packets early to signal congestion.
example: A large upload on a home line can push ping times from 20 ms to 500 ms because of bufferbloat.

definition: Router techniques that drop or mark packets before a buffer is full, keeping queues short and latency low. CoDel and FQ-CoDel are examples.
example: Enabling FQ-CoDel on a home router can keep latency low during big uploads.

definition: Controlled Delay: an active queue management algorithm that drops packets when they have waited too long in the queue. FQ-CoDel (RFC 8290) combines it with fair queueing between flows.
example: FQ-CoDel is the default queueing discipline on many Linux systems.

definition: The fraction of a link's capacity that arriving traffic asks for: average arrival rate times mean packet size, divided by link rate. As it approaches 1 (100%), queues grow without limit.
example: 7,500 packets/s of 1500-byte packets on a 100 Mbit/s link is a traffic intensity of 0.9.

definition: The simplest queueing-theory model: random (Poisson) arrivals, random (exponentially distributed) service times, one server and unlimited waiting room. Its mean wait is ρ/(1 − ρ) service times, where ρ is the utilisation, so it grows sharply near full load.
example: At 50% utilisation an M/M/1 packet waits on average one service time; at 99%, 99.

definition: A model of arrivals that happen independently and at random at a constant average rate, like customers wandering into a shop. It is the "M" for arrivals in M/M/1.
example: If packets arrive as a Poisson process at 1,000 per second, any given millisecond sees one on average, but some see none and some several.

definition: A random time whose short values are most likely but long ones possible, and which has no memory of how long it has already run. M/M/1 assumes service times follow it; fixed-size packets do not.
example: Real packets of one fixed size have constant transmission times, so M/M/1 is only an illustration.

definition: The mathematics of waiting lines: how arrival rate, service rate and randomness determine queue length and waiting time.
example: Queueing theory explains why a link at 95% average load can feel far worse than one at 70%.

definition: A path's data rate multiplied by its round-trip time: how much data must be sent but not yet acknowledged to keep the path full. A sender's window must be at least this big.
example: 1 Gbit/s × 70 ms = 70 Mbit, so 8.75 MB must be in flight.

definition: The limit on how much data a sender may have sent but not yet had acknowledged. As acknowledgements arrive the window "slides" forward and more may be sent. Its size caps throughput at one window per round trip.
example: A 65,535-byte window over a 70 ms round trip allows at most about 7.5 Mbit/s.

definition: The amount of data a TCP receiver says it is willing to accept, advertised in every segment. Without window scaling the field is 16 bits, so at most 65,535 bytes.
example: A receiver advertising 65,535 bytes over a 100 ms RTT limits the sender to about 5.2 Mbit/s.

definition: A TCP option (RFC 7323), agreed during the handshake, that multiplies the 16-bit window field by a power of two so windows can be far larger than 65,535 bytes.
example: With window scaling, a receiver can advertise a window of several megabytes for a long, fast path.

definition: A path with a large bandwidth-delay product: fast and long, so a great deal of data is in flight at once. Such paths need large windows and buffers.
example: A 10 Gbit/s link between continents with a 100 ms RTT holds 125 MB in flight.

definition: The slowest link on a path, which caps the end-to-end throughput however fast the other links are.
example: A 100 Mbit/s broadband line is the bottleneck behind a 1 Gbit/s home network.

definition: Sending data again because it was lost or damaged, or because its acknowledgement did not arrive in time. Retransmitted copies use capacity but do not add to goodput.
example: If 5% of transmissions are retransmissions, only 95% of the payload rate is new data.

definition: Packets that never reach their destination, because a queue overflowed, a check failed or a link failed. TCP treats loss as a sign of congestion.
example: A flaky cable can cause packet loss that forces TCP to retransmit and slow down.

definition: TCP's start-up phase, in which it begins with a small window and roughly doubles it each round trip until it detects loss or reaches a threshold. Short transfers often finish before it ends.
example: A 20 KB response may need a few round trips of slow start before the window is large enough.

definition: The exchange of messages that sets up a connection before data flows. TCP's three-way handshake takes one round trip; a full TLS 1.3 handshake one more, and TLS 1.2 two more.
example: A fresh HTTPS connection with TLS 1.2 spends three round trips on handshakes before the request.

definition: Version 1.3 of Transport Layer Security (RFC 8446). A full TLS 1.3 handshake needs one round trip before the client can send application data, one fewer than a conventional full TLS 1.2 handshake.
example: Upgrading from TLS 1.2 to TLS 1.3 saves one round trip on every new connection.

definition: A TLS 1.3 and QUIC feature letting a returning client send data with its very first message, using keys from an earlier connection. It saves a round trip but the early data can be replayed, so it must be safe to repeat.
example: A client reconnecting to a site it visited yesterday can send a GET request in 0-RTT data.

definition: Reusing keys agreed in an earlier TLS session so a new connection skips the most expensive part of the handshake.
example: A browser returning to a site can resume its TLS session instead of doing a full handshake.

definition: A TLS 1.2 optimisation that lets the client send application data before the handshake fully finishes, saving one round trip.
example: With False Start, a TLS 1.2 connection can send its request after one handshake round trip instead of two.

definition: A TCP extension (RFC 7413) that lets a returning client send data in the very first handshake packet, using a cookie from an earlier connection.
example: TCP Fast Open can save a round trip on repeat connections to the same server.

definition: Sending many requests over one already open connection instead of opening a new one each time, avoiding repeated handshakes.
example: Reusing one HTTPS connection cuts a 600 ms call to about 150 ms on a 150 ms RTT path.

definition: A satellite 35,786 km above the equator that orbits once a day, so it stays over one spot. The distance makes every round trip through it at least about 480 ms.
example: A ship using a geostationary satellite sees RTTs of about half a second.

definition: A point-to-point radio link between line-of-sight towers. Radio in air travels close to the speed of light, faster than light in glass, so microwave routes are used where latency matters most.
example: Trading firms use microwave chains between exchanges to beat fibre by milliseconds.

definition: Keeping several packets, frames or requests in flight at once instead of waiting for each to finish, or be acknowledged, before starting the next. Different links, or the sender and the wait for replies, then overlap in time.
example: Three small packets over three store-and-forward links arrive in 5 ms instead of 9 ms because they pipeline.

definition: The speed of light in a vacuum, about 3 × 10⁸ m/s (299,792,458 m/s exactly). Signals in glass fibre travel at about two-thirds of it; radio in air at almost all of it.
example: Even at the speed of light, a signal needs 133 ms to go once round the Earth's equator.

definition: One signalling element sent for a fixed interval: a voltage level, a light level, or a combination of amplitude and phase. Each symbol can carry several bits if it can take many distinguishable values.
example: A PAM-4 symbol takes one of four voltage levels, so it carries 2 bits.

definition: The number of symbols sent per second, measured in baud (1 baud = one symbol per second). Bit rate equals baud rate times bits per symbol.
example: A 1 Gbaud PAM-4 link carries 2 Gbit/s.

definition: The number of bits sent per second over a link, in bit/s. It equals the symbol rate times the bits each symbol carries, before any coding overhead is removed.
example: 100 Mbaud × 6 bits per symbol = 600 Mbit/s raw bit rate.

definition: Signalling that encodes data in a pulse's amplitude (level). PAM-4 uses 4 levels (2 bits per symbol); 1000BASE-T uses PAM-5 (5 levels) on each of its four pairs.
example: Many 50 and 100 Gbit/s optical lanes use PAM-4.

definition: Quadrature amplitude modulation: encoding data in both the amplitude and the phase of a carrier wave. 16-QAM has 16 combinations (4 bits per symbol) and 1024-QAM has 1024 (10 bits), but denser constellations need a cleaner signal.
example: Wi-Fi 6 can use 1024-QAM close to the access point and drop to 16-QAM further away.

definition: The size (strength) of a signal: how far a voltage or wave swings from its resting level.
example: QAM varies a carrier's amplitude and phase together to encode bits.

definition: Where a repeating wave is in its cycle at a given instant, measured as an angle. Shifting the phase of a carrier is one way to encode data.
example: QAM symbols differ in amplitude, phase, or both.

definition: Varying a signal's amplitude, phase or frequency to carry data. Higher-order modulation packs more bits per symbol but needs a higher signal-to-noise ratio.
example: Wi-Fi drops to a more robust modulation as you walk away from the access point.

definition: Known reference signals mixed in with data so the receiver can measure the channel and stay synchronised. They use capacity without carrying user data.
example: Wi-Fi OFDM reserves some subcarriers as pilots.

definition: Smearing of one symbol's pulse into its neighbours, so they blur together at the receiver. Nyquist's 2B limit assumes pulses shaped to avoid it at the sampling instants.
example: A long cable spreads each pulse, so its tail overlaps the next symbol: intersymbol interference.

definition: A signal or channel whose frequencies start at (or near) zero rather than being shifted up onto a carrier. Wired Ethernet signals are baseband; radio is not.
example: A 3.1 kHz baseband channel passes frequencies from 0 to 3.1 kHz.

definition: The unit of frequency: one cycle per second. Channel bandwidth in the signal sense is measured in hertz: kHz (thousands), MHz (millions), GHz (billions).
example: A Wi-Fi channel 20 MHz wide spans 20 million hertz of spectrum.

definition: The result that an ideal channel B hertz wide can carry at most 2B independent symbols per second without intersymbol interference. With M levels per symbol that is 2B × log₂ M bits per second, ignoring noise.
example: A 3.1 kHz noiseless channel with 4 levels carries at most 12.4 kbit/s.

definition: The highest bit rate a noisy channel can carry with arbitrarily few errors: C = B × log₂(1 + S/N) for bandwidth B and signal-to-noise power ratio S/N. No modulation or coding can beat it.
example: A 20 MHz channel at 30 dB SNR has a capacity of about 199 Mbit/s.

definition: Additive white Gaussian noise: the standard noise model, in which random noise with a bell-curve (Gaussian) spread of values and equal power at all frequencies is simply added to the signal. Shannon's formula assumes it.
example: Thermal noise in a receiver is close to AWGN.

definition: Signal-to-noise ratio: received signal power divided by noise power, usually quoted in decibels. Higher SNR lets a receiver tell more levels apart, so it allows more bits per symbol.
example: 30 dB SNR means the signal is 1000 times more powerful than the noise.

definition: Unwanted random disturbance added to a signal by electronics, interference or the environment. It blurs closely spaced signal levels, which is what limits how many bits each symbol can carry.
example: Doubling a channel's width with fixed noise spectral density doubles its noise power.

definition: A logarithmic unit for a power ratio: 10 × log₁₀ of the ratio. Every 10 dB is a factor of 10 and every 3 dB about a factor of 2, and losses along a path simply add.
example: 24 dB of loss leaves 10^(−2.4) ≈ 0.4% of the power; fibre loss is quoted in dB per kilometre (dB/km).

definition: The inverse of raising to a power: log₂(x) is the power 2 must be raised to to make x, and log₁₀(x) the power of 10. Logarithms turn multiplication into addition, which is why decibels and bits-per-symbol use them.
example: log₂(64) = 6 because 2⁶ = 64; log₁₀(1000) = 3.

definition: Multiple-input multiple-output: using several antennas at each end to send independent data streams on the same channel at once, multiplying capacity when the radio paths differ enough.
example: A 2×2 MIMO Wi-Fi link can carry two spatial streams, roughly doubling its rate.

definition: The weakening of a signal as it travels, measured in decibels. Copper attenuates high frequencies faster; fibre loses about 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm.
example: An 80 km span at 0.2 dB/km attenuates the light by 16 dB, to about 2.5%.

definition: Mapping bits onto the signal sent on the wire in a way that keeps enough transitions for clock recovery and, in some codes, keeps the signal balanced around zero.
example: Manchester coding puts a transition in the middle of every bit.

definition: Mixing the data with a pseudo-random bit sequence so long runs of identical bits become unlikely. It gives statistical, not guaranteed, transition density and balance.
example: 64b/66b relies on scrambling to break up long runs of 0s or 1s.

definition: Non-return-to-zero: the simplest line code, high for 1 and low for 0 for the whole bit. Long runs of the same bit give the receiver no transitions to keep time by.
example: A run of 1,000 zeros in NRZ is one long low level.

definition: Working out the sender's bit timing from the received signal itself, usually from its transitions, when no separate clock wire is sent.
example: A receiver uses each 0-to-1 or 1-to-0 transition to nudge its clock back into step.

definition: Drift of the receiver's idea of "zero" when the signal is not balanced: an AC-coupled link blocks the steady (DC) part of a long run of identical bits. A DC-balanced code sends equal numbers of highs and lows over time to prevent it.
example: Manchester and 8b/10b are DC-balanced; plain NRZ is not.

definition: Connecting circuits through a transformer or capacitor that passes changing (AC) signals but blocks steady (DC) voltage. It isolates equipment electrically but cannot carry a long constant level.
example: Ethernet ports are transformer-coupled, so a long unbalanced run would drift.

definition: A steady current or voltage that does not change direction. In signalling, the "DC component" is the signal's long-term average level.
example: A long run of 1s in NRZ looks like a constant DC level.

definition: A current or voltage that keeps changing direction. AC-coupled links pass only the changing part of a signal.
example: A transformer passes AC but blocks DC.

definition: Two coils of wire on a shared core that pass changing signals magnetically while blocking DC and isolating the two sides. Ethernet ports use small transformers.
example: The transformer inside an RJ45 jack isolates the cable from the computer's circuitry.

definition: A component that stores charge and passes changing signals while blocking steady DC voltage, so it can couple two circuits.
example: High-speed serial links often use capacitors to AC-couple transmitter and receiver.

definition: A line code with a transition in the middle of every bit; in IEEE 802.3's convention 0 is high-then-low and 1 is low-then-high. It is self-clocking and DC-balanced but doubles the signalling rate. 10 Mbit/s Ethernet uses it.
example: Bits 1, 0 become low-high, high-low.

definition: Describes a signal that carries its own timing, so the receiver can recover the clock from it without a separate clock wire.
example: Manchester coding is self-clocking because every bit has a mid-bit transition.

definition: A line code that maps each fixed group of data bits to a longer group of line bits, chosen to guarantee transitions (and sometimes balance) and to leave spare patterns for control.
example: 8b/10b maps every 8 data bits to 10 line bits: 25% overhead.

definition: A block code that sends each 4 data bits as 5 line bits (25% overhead), limiting runs of zeros. It does not by itself guarantee DC balance. 100BASE-TX and FDDI use it.
example: 100 Mbit/s of data becomes 125 million line bits per second.

definition: A block code that sends each 8 data bits as 10 line bits (25% overhead), guaranteeing transitions and DC balance. 1000BASE-X, SATA and early PCIe use it.
example: 1 Gbit/s of data needs 1.25 Gbaud on the line.

definition: A block code that sends each 64 data bits as 66 line bits (3.125% overhead), with scrambling for statistical balance. 10GBASE-R and faster Ethernet use it.
example: 10 Gbit/s of data runs at 10.3125 Gbaud.

definition: Multi-level transmit: a three-level line code that, for each 1, steps to the next level in the repeating cycle 0, +, 0, −, and for each 0 holds its level, lowering the signal's frequency content. 100BASE-TX uses it after 4B/5B.
example: 100BASE-TX sends 125 million MLT-3 symbols per second.

definition: One of the bit patterns a code allows. Line codes leave some patterns unused for control; error-detecting codes are designed so valid codewords differ in several bits.
example: In 4B/5B only 16 of the 32 possible 5-bit patterns carry data.

definition: Fast Ethernet over two pairs of Category 5 twisted pair at 100 Mbit/s, using 4B/5B then MLT-3 at 125 million symbols per second.
example: Older office switches often had 100BASE-TX ports.

definition: Gigabit Ethernet over four pairs of Category 5e or better twisted pair, up to 100 m. It sends PAM-5 at 125 Mbaud on all four pairs in both directions at once, using echo cancellation.
example: A typical laptop's wired port is 1000BASE-T.

definition: The family of gigabit Ethernet PHYs for fibre (such as 1000BASE-SX for multimode and 1000BASE-LX for longer reach), using 8b/10b at 1.25 Gbaud.
example: 1000BASE-SX runs over multimode fibre with 850 nm optics.

definition: 10 Gbit/s Ethernet over twisted pair, supporting 100 m on Category 6a cabling.
example: A server with a 10GBASE-T port can use ordinary RJ45 patch cables up to 100 m on Cat6a.

definition: The family of serial 10 Gbit/s Ethernet PHYs that use 64b/66b coding at 10.3125 Gbaud, including 10GBASE-SR and 10GBASE-LR.
example: 10GBASE-SR and 10GBASE-LR share the 10GBASE-R coding but use different optics.

definition: 10 Gbit/s Ethernet over multimode fibre with 850 nm optics, reaching about 300 m on OM3 and 400 m on OM4.
example: Switches in the same data-centre row are often linked with 10GBASE-SR.

definition: 10 Gbit/s Ethernet over single-mode fibre with 1310 nm optics, rated for up to 10 km.
example: Two buildings 2 km apart can be linked directly with 10GBASE-LR.

definition: The family of Ethernet standards at 10 Gbit/s, over copper and fibre. It and faster Ethernet support only full duplex.
example: 10GbE links between switches never use CSMA/CD.

definition: Fiber Distributed Data Interface: a 100 Mbit/s fibre ring LAN standard of the late 1980s and 1990s, now obsolete. It introduced the 4B/5B code later reused by Fast Ethernet.
example: Campus backbones in the early 1990s often ran FDDI.

definition: Serial ATA: the common interface between computers and disk drives, which uses 8b/10b coding on its serial links.
example: A SATA III link signals at 6 Gbaud and carries 4.8 Gbit/s after 8b/10b.

definition: PCI Express: the high-speed serial expansion bus inside computers. Generations 1 and 2 use 8b/10b coding, generations 3 to 5 use 128b/130b, and generation 6 moved to PAM-4 signalling with forward error correction.
example: A network card plugs into a PCIe slot.

definition: Cable made of pairs of insulated copper wires twisted together. Each pair carries a signal as the voltage difference between its two wires, which, with the twisting, rejects interference and crosstalk.
example: A standard Ethernet patch cable has four twisted pairs.

definition: Grades of twisted-pair cabling defined by how high a frequency they carry cleanly. Cat5e supports gigabit Ethernet; Cat6a supports 10GBASE-T to 100 m.
example: A new office for 10 Gbit/s to the desk would be wired with Cat6a.

definition: Sending a signal as the difference between two wires' voltages. Interference that hits both wires equally cancels when the receiver subtracts them.
example: If noise adds 0.2 V to both wires, their difference is unchanged.

definition: Interference that appears equally on both wires of a pair. A differential receiver rejects it, to the extent the cable and receiver are balanced.
example: A nearby motor induces common-mode noise that a twisted pair largely cancels.

definition: Unwanted coupling of a signal from one wire pair into a neighbouring pair. Twisting pairs at different rates reduces it.
example: Poorly terminated Ethernet cables can fail at high speed because of crosstalk near the connector.

definition: Subtracting a device's own outgoing signal from what it hears on the same wires, so it can receive while transmitting. 1000BASE-T uses it to send both ways on each pair at once.
example: Without echo cancellation a 1000BASE-T port would hear mostly its own transmission.

definition: Cable with a centre conductor inside a cylindrical shield, separated by insulation. It carried early Ethernet and still carries cable TV and cable broadband.
example: Cable broadband reaches homes over coax using DOCSIS.

aliases: Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification
definition: Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification: the standard for broadband internet over cable TV coaxial networks.
example: A cable modem speaks DOCSIS to the provider's equipment.

definition: A thin strand of glass that guides light over long distances with very little loss. It carries most long-distance and data-centre traffic; signals in it travel at about two-thirds of the speed of light.
example: A single-mode fibre can carry a 10 Gbit/s signal 10 km without amplification.

definition: The central glass region of an optical fibre that carries the light, surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index.
example: Multimode cores are 50 or 62.5 µm across; single-mode cores about 9 µm.

definition: The glass layer around a fibre's core, with a slightly lower refractive index, which keeps the light confined to the core.
example: Standard fibre has 125 µm of cladding diameter around its core.

definition: How much slower light travels in a material than in a vacuum: the speed of light divided by the speed in the material. Glass is about 1.45 to 1.47.
example: With an index of 1.47, light covers about 204,000 km per second.

definition: Complete reflection of light hitting the boundary with a lower-index material at a shallow enough angle. It is the simple ray picture of why light stays inside a fibre core.
example: Light inside a multimode core bounces along it by total internal reflection.

definition: One of the distinct patterns in which light can travel along a fibre. Multimode fibre carries many, each with a slightly different path length; single-mode fibre carries one.
example: Different modes arriving at different times smear a pulse: modal dispersion.

definition: Spreading of a light pulse because its light travels along modes (paths) of different length, so parts of it arrive at slightly different times. It limits how fast and how far multimode fibre can run; chromatic dispersion, where different wavelengths travel at different speeds, is a separate effect.
example: Modal dispersion is why multimode fibre reaches only hundreds of metres at 10 Gbit/s.

definition: Fibre with a wide core (50 or 62.5 µm) carrying many modes of light. It uses cheap 850 nm optics but reaches only a few hundred metres at 10 Gbit/s.
example: 10GBASE-SR reaches about 400 m on OM4 multimode fibre.

definition: Fibre with a narrow core that supports one spatial mode, avoiding modal dispersion. With 1310 or 1550 nm lasers it reaches tens of kilometres, and thousands with amplifiers.
example: 10GBASE-LR runs 10 km over single-mode fibre.

definition: Grades of laser-optimised 50 µm multimode fibre. For 10GBASE-SR, OM3 supports about 300 m and OM4 about 400 m.
example: A data centre choosing OM4 gets longer 10 Gbit/s runs than with OM3.

definition: A light source producing a narrow, intense, single-wavelength beam. Long-reach fibre links use lasers; short links can use LEDs or cheap lasers called VCSELs.
example: 1550 nm lasers drive long-haul single-mode links.

definition: Light-emitting diode: a cheap semiconductor light source, used in some short-reach fibre links.
example: Older multimode links at 100 Mbit/s used LED transmitters.

definition: The distance between successive peaks of a wave. For fibre optics it is given in nanometres; different wavelengths can share one fibre without interfering.
example: A DWDM system sends dozens of wavelengths around 1550 nm through one fibre.

definition: Sending many signals through one fibre, each on its own wavelength of light. DWDM (dense WDM) packs dozens of closely spaced wavelengths.
example: A DWDM link with 80 channels of 100 Gbit/s carries 8 Tbit/s on one fibre.

definition: A device that boosts light directly, without converting it to electrical form, so long fibre routes can span thousands of kilometres. EDFAs are the common type.
example: Long undersea cables have optical amplifiers at design-specific intervals, often several tens of kilometres to around 100 km apart.

definition: Erbium-doped fibre amplifier: a length of specially doped fibre, pumped by a laser, that amplifies light around 1550 nm. It adds only a tiny delay.
example: An EDFA can amplify every DWDM wavelength in a fibre at once.

definition: A permanent joint between two fibres, made by fusing or mechanically aligning them. Each splice and connector adds a little loss to the link budget.
example: A fusion splice typically loses well under 0.1 dB.

definition: The difference between a transmitter's launch power and the weakest signal the receiver can use. Fibre loss, connectors, splices and margins must all fit within it.
example: With 10 dB of budget, a link at 0.4 dB/km plus 2 dB of connectors can run about 20 km.

definition: The optical power a transmitter puts into the fibre, usually in dBm (decibels relative to 1 milliwatt).
example: Fibre loss is measured relative to the launch power.

definition: The weakest signal a receiver can still decode at an acceptable error rate.
example: A link works only if launch power minus losses stays above receiver sensitivity.

definition: How many times slower than the speed of light a pulse (rather than a single wave) travels in a fibre. It is the right index for propagation delay; about 1.468 for typical single-mode fibre at 1550 nm.
example: With a group index of 1.47, pulses travel at about 2.04 × 10⁸ m/s.

definition: The speed at which a pulse, and so the data it carries, travels through a medium: the speed of light divided by the group index.
example: In standard fibre the group velocity is about 0.68 of the speed of light.

definition: A widely deployed single-mode fibre product from Corning. Its data sheet lists a typical group index of 1.4682 at 1550 nm.
example: Propagation calculations for real routes use the installed fibre's data-sheet group index.

definition: The speed of a signal in a cable as a fraction of the speed of light. It depends on the cable's construction, especially its insulation.
example: A twisted-pair cable with velocity factor 0.72, such as Belden 2433, carries signals at 72% of the speed of light.

definition: A Belden Category 6+ enhanced twisted-pair cable (4 bonded pairs, U/UTP, plenum-rated) whose data sheet specifies a nominal velocity of propagation of 72% of the speed of light.
example: Signals in Belden 2433 travel faster than light in typical glass fibre (about 68% of c).

definition: An electrical insulator, such as the plastic around each wire of a twisted pair or between a coaxial cable's conductors. Its properties set the cable's velocity factor.
example: Foam dielectric gives a higher velocity factor than solid plastic.

definition: The slow average speed at which electrons creep through a conductor carrying current, typically millimetres per second or less. It is not the speed of the signal, which is an electromagnetic wave.
example: The signal in a copper cable travels at most of the speed of light, though the electrons barely move.

definition: Optical fibre that guides light mostly through an air-filled core, so pulses travel close to the speed of light in air, faster than in solid glass.
example: Hollow-core fibre can cut propagation delay by roughly a third compared with solid glass.

definition: Microsoft's cloud computing platform. Microsoft has reported deploying hollow-core fibre in its Azure network.
example: Azure regions are linked by Microsoft's own fibre network.

definition: A transmission medium, such as a radio channel or an old coaxial Ethernet cable, used by several devices that must take turns.
example: Every Wi-Fi device on one channel shares the same medium.

definition: When two wireless devices can both reach an access point but cannot hear each other, so neither can tell that the other is transmitting and their signals collide at the access point.
example: Laptops at opposite ends of a house may be hidden nodes to each other.

aliases: carrier-sense multiple access with collision avoidance
definition: Carrier-sense multiple access with collision avoidance: Wi-Fi's rule for sharing the channel. A station listens and waits a random backoff before sending, because radios cannot detect collisions while transmitting.
example: A Wi-Fi station that hears the channel busy waits for it to go idle, then a random number of slots.

definition: The weakening of a radio signal spreading out in empty space: power falls with the square of distance, so each doubling of distance costs about 6 dB. Walls and reflections change real coverage.
example: Moving from 5 m to 10 m from an antenna in free space loses about 6 dB.

definition: How much an antenna concentrates power in particular directions compared with radiating equally in all directions, in decibels.
example: A directional antenna with 15 dB of gain can reach much further along its beam.

definition: A radio signal reaching the receiver by several routes (direct and reflected) with different delays, so the copies interfere. OFDM and MIMO cope with it.
example: Indoors, Wi-Fi signals bounce off walls and arrive several times.

definition: Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing: splitting a wide channel into many narrow subcarriers, each carrying slow symbols. Long symbols tolerate multipath echoes. Wi-Fi, 4G and 5G use it.
example: A 20 MHz Wi-Fi 6 channel is divided into 256 subcarriers, 78.125 kHz apart.

definition: Rapid changes in received radio strength as the device or its surroundings move, caused mainly by multipath interference.
example: Moving a phone a few centimetres can move it out of a fade.

definition: Choosing the modulation and coding (and so the bit rate) to suit current radio conditions: dense, fast schemes when SNR is high, robust, slower ones when it falls.
example: A Wi-Fi link may adapt from 600 Mbit/s near the router to 60 Mbit/s two rooms away.

definition: Communication in both directions but only one at a time. Radios on one channel and shared-cable Ethernet work this way.
example: A walkie-talkie is half duplex: press to talk, release to listen.

definition: Communication in both directions at the same time. Modern switched Ethernet links are full duplex, so there are no collisions.
example: A full-duplex 1 Gbit/s link can carry 1 Gbit/s each way at once.

definition: A device that runs a Wi-Fi network, connecting wireless devices to each other and to the wired network.
example: A large office has many access points, each covering part of the floor.

definition: A home or office Wi-Fi system of several nodes that relay traffic wirelessly to each other to extend coverage. Relaying uses airtime, so it is not a guaranteed speed-up.
example: Adding a mesh node in the far room may raise signal strength there.

definition: The IEEE standard that defines Ethernet: its frame format, MAC rules and physical layers. Its original frame format put a length where Ethernet II puts the EtherType.
example: An EtherType field value of 1500 or less is read as an IEEE 802.3 length, not a protocol type.

definition: Logical Link Control: the IEEE 802.2 header that identifies the payload protocol in original 802.3-format frames, which carry a length instead of an EtherType.
example: Spanning tree BPDUs are carried in 802.3 frames with an LLC header.

definition: Extra filler bytes added to a frame or message that carry no information: to reach a minimum size (Ethernet pads payloads shorter than 46 bytes so every frame is at least 64 bytes), to align data to a block size, or to hide a message's true length.
example: A 28-byte ARP message gets 18 bytes of padding.

definition: The smallest legal Ethernet frame, 64 bytes from destination address to FCS. It was set so that, on shared CSMA/CD Ethernet, a sender is still transmitting when news of a collision at the far end returns.
example: At 10 Mbit/s a 64-byte frame takes 51.2 µs to send, which bounded the size of a collision domain.

definition: A device's or link's rate counted in packets (or frames) rather than bits. Small packets mean more packets per second for the same bit rate, so per-packet work becomes the limit.
example: A 10 Gbit/s link full of minimum frames carries about 14.88 million packets per second.

definition: The 48-bit link-layer address of an Ethernet or Wi-Fi interface, written as six hex bytes such as 3c:22:fb:11:22:33. It identifies the interface on the local link only; routers rewrite frames with new MAC addresses at every hop.
example: An Ethernet header starts with the destination MAC address, then the source MAC address.

definition: Base-16 notation using digits 0–9 and a–f; each hex digit is 4 bits, so a byte is two hex digits. Prefixed 0x in code.
example: 0x3c is binary 0011 1100, decimal 60.

definition: Organisationally unique identifier: a 24-bit number the IEEE assigns to an organisation. With an MA-L (large) block, it forms the first three bytes of the organisation's MAC addresses.
example: 00:1b:21 is an OUI; the vendor numbers the remaining three bytes itself.

definition: The least significant bit of a MAC address's first byte: 0 for an individual (unicast) address, 1 for a group (multicast or broadcast) address. A quick check: the second hex digit is odd for multicast.
example: In 01:00:5e:00:00:fb the first byte 0x01 has its I/G bit set, so it is multicast.

definition: The second-least significant bit of a MAC address's first byte: 0 for a universally administered (vendor-assigned) address, 1 for a locally administered one.
example: 0xda is 1101 1010: U/L is 1 (local) and I/G is 0 (unicast).

definition: A MAC address set by software or an administrator rather than assigned by the manufacturer, marked by U/L bit = 1. Private (randomised) Wi-Fi addresses are locally administered.
example: A locally administered unicast address has a second hex digit of 2, 6, A or E.

definition: A MAC address assigned by the manufacturer under an IEEE OUI, marked by U/L bit = 0, and intended to be globally unique.
example: 3c:22:fb:11:22:33 has U/L = 0, so it is universally administered.

definition: Using a random, locally administered MAC address instead of the hardware one, often a different one per Wi-Fi network, to make tracking harder. It can break MAC allow-lists.
example: An iPhone may join a network as da:a1:19:40:0b:7e rather than the address printed in its settings.

definition: A list of permitted MAC addresses that a network uses to admit devices. It is weak security because MAC addresses can be changed or copied.
example: A randomised MAC address will be refused by an allow-list that only knows the hardware address.

definition: An address scheme with no structure saying where a device is, like MAC addresses. Flat addresses work on a LAN but cannot be summarised for internet-wide routing.
example: A router cannot aggregate MAC addresses by location, but it can aggregate IP prefixes.

definition: The leading bits of an IP address shared by a whole network, written like 192.168.1.0/24. Routers forward on prefixes, which can be aggregated hierarchically.
Carrier-sense multiple access: sharing a medium by listening first and transmitting only when it seems idle. CSMA/CD (Ethernet) and CSMA/CA (Wi-Fi) add different ways of handling collisions.
example: Both classic Ethernet and Wi-Fi are CSMA systems.

aliases: carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection
definition: Carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection: classic shared Ethernet's rule for taking turns. Listen before sending, keep listening while sending, and on a collision stop, send a jam signal and retry after a random backoff.
example: Modern full-duplex switched Ethernet switches CSMA/CD off.

definition: Listening to the medium before transmitting and waiting if another station is already sending.
example: Carrier sense alone cannot stop two stations that start within the propagation delay of each other.

definition: Noticing, while transmitting, that the signal on the wire differs from what you are sending, which means another station transmitted at the same time.
example: Wi-Fi radios cannot do collision detection because their own signal drowns out others.

definition: Two stations on a shared medium transmitting at overlapping times, so both frames are garbled and must be resent.
example: On a hub-based 10 Mbit/s LAN, collisions rose sharply as traffic grew.

definition: A collision detected after the first 64 bytes (512 bit-times) of a frame have been sent, which should never happen on a correctly built network. It points to a duplex mismatch or an over-long segment.
example: A switch port counting late collisions often has a duplex mismatch.

definition: A 32-bit signal a CSMA/CD station sends after detecting a collision, so every station on the segment notices the collision.
example: After hearing the jam signal, both senders back off before retrying.

definition: Waiting a random number of slot times before retrying, where the range doubles after each collision on the same frame (0–1, 0–3, 0–7, … up to 0–1023). It spreads retries out as load grows.
example: After its third collision a station waits 0 to 7 slot times.

definition: Ethernet's basic time unit for collisions and backoff: 512 bit-times at 10 and 100 Mbit/s (51.2 µs at 10 Mbit/s), 4096 bit-times for historical half-duplex gigabit.
example: A station that picks 5 after a collision waits 5 slot times.

definition: An old physical-layer device that repeated every incoming bit out of every other port, so all connected hosts shared one collision domain. Switches replaced hubs.
example: Two hosts sending at once through a hub caused a collision.

definition: A device partway along a link that boosts or regenerates the signal to extend its reach, adding a little delay but no frame processing. Ethernet repeaters and hubs regenerate bits; the "repeaters" of undersea cables are optical amplifiers.
example: Repeater delays counted towards the classic Ethernet collision-domain limits.

definition: A historical half-duplex gigabit Ethernet trick: padding short frames on the wire with special non-data symbols to a 4096-bit slot so collisions could still be detected over useful distances.
example: Carrier extension was never needed for full-duplex gigabit links.

definition: The set of stations whose transmissions can collide with each other, such as everything on one hub. Each full-duplex switch port is its own collision-free link.
example: Replacing a hub with a switch gives every port its own collision domain.

definition: A link where one end runs full duplex and the other half duplex. The half-duplex side sees "collisions" whenever both send, causing errors and poor throughput under load while light traffic seems fine.
example: Forcing a server to full duplex while its switch port negotiates half can cause a duplex mismatch.

definition: The exchange by which two Ethernet ends agree on speed and duplex when the link comes up. Best practice is auto-negotiation at both ends.
example: If one end is forced to full duplex, the auto-negotiating end may fall back to half duplex.

definition: Received frames that fail their FCS check, or whose length is not a whole number of bytes. Counters for them point to cabling faults, interference or duplex mismatches.
example: A NIC showing climbing CRC errors suggests a damaged cable or a mismatch.

definition: A received frame shorter than the 64-byte minimum, typically a fragment left when a transmission was cut short by a collision.
example: A half-duplex peer aborting transmissions can make the other side count runt frames.

definition: A link-layer device that connects many Ethernet links and forwards each frame only towards its destination, learning where hosts are from their source MAC addresses. It is the modern form of a multi-port bridge.
example: An office switch with 48 ports forwards a frame from port 3 only to the port where the destination was last seen.

definition: A link-layer device that joins network segments and forwards frames between them by destination MAC address. A switch is a many-port bridge; standards still call them bridges.
example: IEEE 802.1Q is formally the standard for bridges and bridged networks.

definition: The table a switch builds mapping each learned MAC address (per VLAN) to the port it was last seen on. It is often called the CAM table after the content-addressable memory used to search it fast.
example: After seeing a frame from host A on port 1, the switch adds "A → port 1" to its MAC address table.

definition: A switch recording, for every frame it receives, that the source MAC address is reachable through the arrival port. It is how a switch fills its MAC address table without configuration.
example: A host that sends one frame is immediately learned on its port.

definition: Sending a copy of something out of every eligible interface except the one it arrived on. A switch floods a frame to every port in the VLAN when its destination is unknown, broadcast or (by default) multicast; link-state routers flood routing updates to every neighbour in the same way.
example: A switch that has never seen host B floods a frame for B to all its other ports.

definition: Removing a dynamic MAC table entry that has not been refreshed by traffic for a configured time, commonly 300 seconds, so the table tracks moves and stays small.
example: A laptop unplugged for ten minutes will have aged out of the switch's table.

definition: A table entry configured by an administrator rather than learned, which does not age out.
example: A static MAC entry pins a server's address to one switch port.

definition: The port a frame arrives on (ingress) as opposed to the port it leaves by (egress). A switch never floods a frame back out of its ingress port in ordinary bridging.
example: A broadcast arriving on port 3 is flooded to every port except its ingress port, 3.

definition: A switch watching multicast group-membership messages so it can send multicast frames only to ports with interested receivers instead of flooding them.
example: With IGMP snooping, an IPTV stream reaches only the set-top boxes that joined it.

definition: A special switch mode that may send a frame back out of the port it arrived on, used for example with virtual machines behind one port. Ordinary bridging never does this.
example: Hairpin mode lets two VMs on one host talk through the external switch.

definition: An attack that sends frames from huge numbers of fake source MAC addresses to fill a switch's MAC table, hoping the switch will then flood unknown-unicast traffic to the attacker.
example: A tool sending 100,000 frames per second with random source MACs can exhaust a small switch's table.

definition: Switch features that limit how many MAC addresses a port may learn and what happens on violation (drop, alert or shut the port). They contain MAC flooding attacks.
example: Limiting a desk port to 2 learned MAC addresses stops one host flooding the table.

definition: Forging an identity field, such as a source MAC or IP address, so traffic appears to come from someone else.
example: A MAC flooding tool sends frames with spoofed source addresses.

definition: Virtual LAN: a separate, isolated broadcast domain created in switch configuration, so one physical switch fabric can carry several LANs. Traffic between VLANs must be routed.
example: Staff, guest Wi-Fi and phones can share switches but sit in three VLANs.

definition: The IEEE standard for VLANs and bridging. It defines the 4-byte VLAN tag inserted after the source MAC address, and now also contains the spanning-tree protocols.
example: An 802.1Q-tagged frame carries TPID 0x8100 followed by a 12-bit VLAN ID.

definition: The 4 bytes 802.1Q inserts after the source MAC address: TPID (2 bytes), then PCP, DEI and the VLAN ID (2 bytes). Priority tagging uses VLAN ID 0 to carry only a priority.
example: Adding a VLAN tag to a 1518-byte frame makes it 1522 bytes.

definition: Tag protocol identifier: the first 16 bits of a VLAN tag, sitting where the EtherType would be. 0x8100 marks an 802.1Q tag and 0x88A8 an 802.1ad outer tag.
example: A receiver seeing 0x8100 after the source MAC knows a VLAN tag follows.

definition: Priority code point: the 3-bit priority field in a VLAN tag (values 0–7), used for quality of service.
example: Voice traffic is often marked with PCP 5.

definition: Drop eligible indicator: a 1-bit field in a VLAN tag marking a frame that may be dropped first under congestion.
example: A provider can mark traffic above a customer's contracted rate with DEI = 1.

definition: VLAN identifier: the 12-bit field naming a frame's VLAN. Of its 4096 values, 0 means priority-only and 4095 is reserved, leaving 4094 assignable VLANs (1–4094).
example: A frame tagged with VID 20 belongs to VLAN 20.

definition: Quality of service: treating some traffic preferentially, for example queueing voice ahead of bulk downloads, based on markings such as PCP.
example: QoS can keep a video call smooth while a backup runs.

definition: A switch port that belongs to one VLAN and exchanges ordinary untagged frames with the host plugged into it.
example: A desk PC on an access port in VLAN 10 never sees a VLAN tag.

definition: A switch port that carries several VLANs, usually distinguishing them with 802.1Q tags, to another switch, a router or a hypervisor.
example: The link between two floor switches is a trunk port carrying all ten VLANs.

definition: The VLAN that untagged frames on a trunk port are assigned to. Depending on configuration it may also be sent tagged, or untagged frames may be refused.
example: A trunk with native VLAN 1 puts any untagged frame it receives into VLAN 1.

definition: A VLAN reserved for IP phones on an otherwise ordinary access port, typically tagged so the phone's traffic is separated and prioritised.
example: A desk phone with a PC behind it uses the voice VLAN while the PC stays untagged.

definition: A switch that can also route IP packets between VLANs in hardware.
example: Inter-VLAN traffic in an office core often goes through a layer 3 switch rather than a separate router.

definition: A switch or access-point setting that stops devices on the same VLAN or Wi-Fi network from talking directly to each other at layer 2.
example: Hotel Wi-Fi uses client isolation so guests cannot reach each other's laptops.

definition: Provider bridging ("Q-in-Q"): stacking a second, outer VLAN tag (TPID 0x88A8) in front of a customer's 802.1Q tag so a provider can carry many customers' VLANs.
example: A carrier uses 802.1ad to keep each customer's 4094 VLANs separate inside its own.

definition: The 24-bit identifier in a VXLAN header naming a virtual layer 2 network, allowing about 16 million of them instead of 4094 VLANs.
example: Each tenant in a cloud data centre can get its own VNI.

definition: Ethernet frames larger than the standard 1500-byte MTU, typically about 9000 bytes. They cut per-packet work but are not part of the IEEE standard, and every device on the path must support them.
example: Storage networks often run jumbo frames between servers and arrays.

definition: A hardware signal that makes the CPU stop and handle an event, such as a network card receiving packets. Interrupt moderation batches several packets per interrupt.
example: With interrupt moderation, a NIC might raise one interrupt for every 50 received frames.

definition: Work a network card does in hardware on the CPU's behalf, such as computing checksums or splitting large sends into segments.
example: With segmentation offload, the kernel hands the NIC 64 KB and the NIC sends 45 full-size segments.

definition: Two devices or links on one path configured with different MTUs, so packets the sender thinks are legal are too big for some hop. Unless fragmentation or path-MTU discovery fixes it, large packets vanish.
example: A jumbo-frame server sending 9000-byte packets across a 1500-byte link hits an MTU mismatch.
